book: 037 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West

chapters.file: ch03 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy.md
ch05 - Ideas and Images of Oz.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Oz endures because it is not one story but a shifting plurality of tales (storyteller Chris Chandler's point, likening it to the Iliad), which each reader can enter through any character, from the Lion to, after Gregory Maguire, the Wicked Witch herself. It models the volume's method with a small logical puzzle about 'there's no place like home'—the phrase is negative because Dorothy herself is part of what home means, so Kansas has a new Dorothy—and previews the book's recurring questions: the Yellow Brick Road as a many-meaninged journey metaphor, the virtues of brain, heart, and courage, evil (why must a little girl kill the Witch?), and the reality-status of Oz versus Kansas.

chapters.file: ch06 - The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy.md
ch07 - I - Are You a Good Witch or a Bad Witch.md
ch08 - There’s No Place Like Home.md
chapters.relation: Luke Dick stages Immanuel Kant as the 'Supreme Critical Chancellor of Munchkinland' and runs the film through Kantian ethics: against hedonism, utilitarianism, and command-based religion, the formula of universalizability condemns the Wizard's lies and his use of the companions as mere means, while the ends-in-themselves principle raises the awkward case of Glinda and Dorothy keeping the dead Witch of the East's ruby slippers. Judging the characters, the Lion's rescue of Dorothy is morally praiseworthy (duty against strong inclination), the brainless Scarecrow falls outside Kant's jurisdiction, and the sentimental Tin Man is pre-emptively condemned. The chapter finally rebels against its Chancellor: cases like returning the slippers, or Toto versus Almira Gulch, show that a world of absolute morality lies only 'somewhere over the rainbow,' and real moral life in Kansas needs Baum's Tin Man heart reconciled with Kantian duty.

chapters.file: ch09 - Dorothy Growing Up in the Land of Oz.md
chapters.relation: McCall and Auxier use Aristotle's virtue ethics to unpack the Wizard's claim to be 'a good man but a bad wizard' and to argue that no external token—the diploma, heart watch, or medal—can confer virtue, which is cultivated only through practice and experience. Each companion lacks something specific: the Scarecrow the intellectual virtues and phronesis, the Tin Man the feelings and stable states of character that regulate emotion, the Lion the sophrosyne that balances thinking and feeling into courage as the mean between recklessness and cowardice. Aristotle's three grades of friendship (utility, pleasure, virtue) frame the companions' bond with Dorothy, and MacIntyre's account of virtues internal to practices explains why the Wizard's public recognition still matters. Dorothy herself begins as the child Aristotle says cannot yet be virtuous—fleeing Miss Gulch in Kansas—but by defending Toto against the Lion and leading the quest she grows into a responsible moral agent, which is what her delayed homecoming requires.

chapters.file: ch10 - And Your Little Dog Too!.md
chapters.relation: Altamura and Fritzman argue the film has the tripartite structure of Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit: gray Kansas is a partial truth (thesis), 'somewhere over the rainbow' the antithesis, and the synthesis is Dorothy's discovery that the home she yearned for was Kansas all along—a truth that emerges only through misrecognition, which is why Glinda cannot simply tell her the slippers' power. They read 'Over the Rainbow' through Hegel's 'unhappy consciousness' and side with Hegel's one world against the Kantian two-worlds reading (Kansas as the knowable island, Oz as the unknowable beyond) that they put in the mouths of heckling 'bullies' and detect in Rushdie. Against Rushdie's line that the companions 'already possess what they seek,' they insist the trio really were hollow men who became brainy, tender, and brave through the journey, the Wizard's trinkets supplying Hegelian public recognition. From the Philosophy of History they cast Dorothy as a world-historical individual whose unintentional destruction of both Witches and exposure of the Wizard advances Oz's freedom—Toto's deliberate pulling of the curtain included.

chapters.file: ch11 - Dorothy and the Art of War.md
chapters.relation: The Bells read Baum's book against Bleeding Kansas and John Brown: 1900 readers, they argue, heard 'Kansas' as the slave-or-free question, making Dorothy the Great Emancipator who frees the Munchkins, the Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman, the Winkies, and finally herself from the Witch's servitude. They pair her with Socrates, recasting the Republic's opening scene at Cephalus's slave-owning mansion (Thrasymachus's 'injustice on a sufficiently large scale' pays) as an abolitionist confrontation, and quoting the Phaedo's claim that philosophy is practicing for death to explain why vastly outnumbered reformers—Socrates, Brown at Harpers Ferry and Osawatomie, Dorothy facing the Witch's forty wolves, forty crows, bee swarms, and Winkie army—do not fear the odds. The shared moral: the love of wisdom, pursued in a community of inquirers, charms away the fear of death, which is why tyrants and slave-owners, whose own best part is enslaved, live in terror and cannot sleep at night.

Curry argues that The Wiz, the all-Black 1978 remake, dramatizes the acquisition of a distinctively Black 'racial virtue'—a habitual excellence defined in quasi-Aristotelian terms and grounded in W.E.B. Du Bois's picture of races as 'vast families' bound by common history and a divinely rooted race feeling (with Alexander Crummell and William H. Ferris as supporting race theorists). Dorothy, a Harlem kindergarten teacher who has never been south of 125th Street, lacks knowledge of self, and each companion personifies a virtue she must claim: the newspaper-stuffed Scarecrow, whose crows' 'crow commandments' and song 'You Can't Win' embody internalized racist miseducation; the Tin Man's capacity for feeling; and Fleetwood Coupe de Ville's courage outside the New York Public Library, glossed through Ferris's call for 'lion-like men.' Evillene's sweatshop creed that 'suffering is food for the soul' personifies the redemptive-suffering myth and failed-integrationism the chapter rejects, while Glinda's 'believe in yourself' and 'A Brand New Day' make honest admittance of racial reality the precondition of 'co-authoring' the world.

chapters.file: ch13 - II - If I Only Had a Mind.md

chapters.relation: Patton turns the Tin Woodman's backstory—the enchanted axe that costs Nick Chopper his legs, arms, torso and heart, then his head, each replaced by the tinsmith—into a cyborg thought experiment about how much of a person can be swapped out before the person is gone. After a framing nod to Plato's Republic on censoring frightening tales (his father's ban on 'mental violence' fantasy), he brings in Derek Parfit: the R-relation, the 'My Division' brain-split, and the Branch-Line teletransportation case are mapped onto the Woodman (including a hypothetical straw-bodied second Nick) to argue that survival gets different answers from first-person and third-person perspectives. The closing wildcat episode, where the tinned Woodman neatly decapitates a wildcat to save a field mouse, is offered as textual evidence that the tin head failed to preserve moral consistency—so the original Nick Chopper is gone for good, and the Scarecrow's shared brain explains why the two friends later refuse to part.

chapters.file: ch15 - “Here, Here, What’s All This Jabber-wapping When There’s Work to Be Done ”.md
chapters.relation: Tschaepe reads Professor Marvel and the Wizard as skilled givers of 'folk explanations'—stories about desires, beliefs, and feelings that work where logical, scientific, or mechanistic explanations fail—because each explanation is fitted to the pragmatic considerations of its audience and problem. With the companions the Wizard works through a failed dualist argument (a brain is not a mind) for the Scarecrow, an abbreviated Stoic ataraxy pitch for the Tin Man, and Aristotle's discretion-is-valor point for the Lion, settling in each case on folk psychology plus a token (Th.D. diploma, heart-shaped clock, Legion of Courage medal) that supplies the recognition actually needed. Dorothy, whose desire for home is real rather than mistaken, gets no folk explanation from anybody: she must combine the heel-tapping instruction with her own articulated desire—'there's no place like home'—which the chapter treats as pragmatically, not logically, effective.

chapters.file: ch16 - III - I’ve a Feeling We’re Not in Kansas Anymore.md

chapters.relation: Auxier gives three theories of why water melts the Wicked Witch, one for each register of Oz: as dream (Bergson's account of dreams as memory explains the fire/water effect-swap), as Baum's fairytale (Susanne Langer's presentational symbols make dryness-wickedness versus water-as-life the tale's moral physics), and as Gregory Maguire's possible world, where the philosophy of language takes over. He narrates Frege's sense/reference distinction—mayor of the Munchkins—to explain how fiction can support truth and falsity ('Dorothy melts the Witch' true, 'Dorothy tried to melt her' false), then deploys Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment: 'water' in Oz is XYZ while Kansas water is H2O, so Elphaba's word 'water' does not mean what Dorothy's does, and meanings just aren't in the head. Elphaba—the unique being straddling two worlds, killed by H2O she cannot name and terrified by dreams of oceans—is offered as an even stronger argument for Putnam's semantic externalism than Twin Earth's molecule-for-molecule doppelgangers.

chapters.file: ch18 - Conscious Unity “There’s No Place Like Home”.md
chapters.relation: McLachlan maps the whole story onto Schelling's romantic eschatology: gray Kansas is the Ungrund, the boring unconscious unity; the tornado (and Dorothy Gale as 'the gale') is the alienating rupture; and 'there's no place like home' is conscious unity regained through love of concrete, limiting others—richer than the unity she left because it now contains real relationships. Each companion's quest begins in egoism (the Scarecrow as an almost perfect Platonist, all disembodied contemplation like the spider-watching Spinoza; the Tin Man's self-loving imperviousness to pain), while evil in Oz—Miss Gulch's totalizing order, the Witches' slave states, the hidden Wizard—is Schelling's second evil: the attempt to control everything and abolish the freedom of others. Against escape-eschatologies (Plato's shadow-world, Bunyan's Pilgrim who flees his family crying 'eternal life,' Dante turning from Beatrice to the divine light), the Schellingian lesson is that even God becomes personal through relation—which is why the Dainty China Princess's refusal to be a mantel ornament marks the exact point of Dorothy's education in love.

Dunn contrasts Baum's book, where evil is wonderfully 'small'—Dorothy melts the Witch in a fit of righteous anger at a stolen Silver Shoe, and personal plus social virtues (kindness repaid by the field-mice Queen) reliably conquer it—with the 1939 film, which smuggles back the 'heartaches and nightmares' Baum banished and resolves the Witch only by an accidental stroke of luck. He sorts Oz's harms into moral evils (the Witch's enslavements, the Wizard's frauds) and natural evils (the cyclone, the Deadly Poppy Field), cites Hume's catalogue of the world's ills, and observes that Baum needs neither Kant's postulate of God and a future life to join virtue with happiness nor John Hick's 'vale of soul-making' theodicy—Oz simply delivers the reward. Dorothy's abundant virtue at age five rebukes Aristotle (children, he says, cannot be virtuous or happy) and instead embodies Rousseau's Emile, natural goodness uncorrupted by civilization, while Chesterton's Doctrine of Conditional Joy and Tolkien's insistence on serious, non-technological magic frame the Old-World Christian outlook that Baum's demystified American fairy tale—and the movie's ending—quietly betray.

Auxier uses the Wizard's demand that Dorothy kill the Witch to split 'ought' from 'can'—ethics from the metaphysics and logic of possibility—and then asks whether Oz is a genuinely possible world. He explains David Lewis's modal realism (every genuine possibility actual in its own causally isolated world) through counterfactuals about which network aired the film, dissolves the silver-versus-ruby slippers conflict by assigning book-Oz and film-Oz to different possible worlds, and argues that since no flat contradiction can be eked out of the Oz stories, Lewis is committed to Oz's being real—though Maguire's inter-world travel and Elphaba's hybrid, soul-less trans-world identity (her counterpart in our world being, playfully, Dorothy) stretch Lewis's 'counterparts' doctrine to its limit. Peirce supplies the closing caution, with Boole, that logic is a set of norms for how we can and ought to think rather than a proven mirror of other worlds, so believing in Oz's full reality remains permissible fun rather than an obligation.

holes.name: Race Feeling (races as vast families)
holes.what: Du Bois and Crummell's idea that races are 'vast families' bound by common history, impulses, and an inherited, quasi-sacred 'race feeling' that links individual self-realization to racial advancement.
holes.why: Chapter 12's central claim is that The Wiz stages Dorothy's cultivation of exactly this racial feeling—knowledge, feeling, courage, admittance—as a Black racial virtue, a concept no existing taxonomy slug (not even double-consciousness) captures.

holes.name: Susanne Langer
holes.what: American philosopher (1895–1985) of mind, art, and symbolism who distinguished presentational (image-based) symbols from discursive (linguistic) thought and analyzed how dreams, fairy tales, and myths transform symbols.
holes.why: Chapter 17 builds two of its three explanations of the Witch's melting—Oz as dream and Oz as fairytale—directly on Langer's quoted theory of symbols, and credits her (with Bergson) against the analytic tradition.

holes.name: F.W.J. Schelling
holes.what: German idealist (1770–1854) whose philosophy of freedom, nature, and love treats God and self as developing through alienation and reconciliation rather than as static perfections.
holes.why: Chapter 18 is built entirely on Schelling's Of Human Freedom—quoting the Ungrund, the split of the groundless, and love as conscious unity—to read Dorothy's journey as a romantic eschatology.

holes.name: Romantic Eschatology (Ungrund, alienation, conscious unity)
holes.what: Schelling's three-stage pattern of the journey: unconscious unity (the groundless Ungrund), fall into egoistic alienation, and return to unity through love that preserves real, limiting others.
holes.why: Chapter 18 maps each stage onto Dorothy's story—gray Kansas, the tornado and selfish quests, and the love-tinged homecoming—so the applied framework itself needs a slug distinct from Hegel's dialectic.

holes.name: Eucatastrophe (the good catastrophe)
holes.what: Tolkien's term for the sudden, miraculous joyous turn at a story's climax that rescues the protagonists when their own efforts cannot—a glimpse of grace beyond tragedy.
holes.why: Chapter 19's pivot is that the film needs a eucatastrophic accident to defeat the Witch while Baum's book needs none, marking the difference between Old-World supernatural dependence and Baum's self-reliant optimism.
